title: Agent access
summary: Every public deliverable stays reachable and readable by the AI agents and search crawlers that find content for people: search indexes, and the fetchers an assistant sends when a person asks about a page. A site may opt out of training crawlers, and never blocks the search-index or user-initiated classes. This names the agent fetchers by token, operator and class, and the robots.txt, edge and probe rules that keep search-index and user-initiated fetchers admitted. Read it when writing robots.txt, adding a WAF, CDN or bot-management rule, or checking whether agents reach a site.
applies_to: Any public web deliverable: a site, web app or HTTP API reachable on the public internet, whatever stack serves it.

classes.search-index: Crawls to build a search index that answers cite and link to. Blocking it removes the site from that operator's search results and AI answers.
classes.user-initiated: Fetches a page when a person asks an assistant about it, at the moment they ask. Several operators document that these fetchers may ignore robots.txt, because a person made the request.
classes.training: Collects content for model training or a bulk web corpus, or is a robots.txt control token for that use. A site may opt out of this class without leaving search indexes or agent answers.
classes.link-preview: Fetches a shared link's title, description and image to render a preview card.

agent_fetchers.note: May bypass robots.txt when performing security or integrity checks.

A robots.txt control token only: no request carries it. Google crawls with its other user agents, and a group naming Google-Extended governs whether that content trains and grounds Gemini models. It does not affect Google Search.
Follows the Googlebot group when robots.txt names Googlebot and not Applebot.
A robots.txt control token only: it crawls no pages. A group naming it governs whether Applebot's crawl trains Apple's foundation models; pages it disallows can still appear in search results.
Amazon documents that its crawl may train Amazon AI models. Amzn-SearchBot and Amzn-User carry search and live answers and train no generative model.
Builds Common Crawl's open web corpus.

probe.expect: One request per path per token of a probed class, the token in the User-Agent header, and one baseline request per path whose User-Agent names no roster token. Each tokened request answers the status the baseline gets on the same path, and never a 401, 403 or 429 or a challenge that the baseline does not get. Where /robots.txt answers 200, the document lets each token fetch /. A tokened request the edge blocks through a rule keyed on the operator's published IP ranges or a verified-bot signal comes from outside those ranges, so the block is expected: confirm that rule under edge-admits-agents and record the result as explained, not as a violation.

rules.summary: The `User-agent: *` group leaves public content open. A named group may disallow public content only for training-class tokens, and no group blocks a search-index or user-initiated token from public content, so access never depends on an agent being named. RFC 9309 applies the `*` group only to a crawler no group names, so a named group repeats any `*` Disallow of a non-public path the site relies on.

/robots.txt answers 200 with Content-Type text/plain and a robots document. A host that serves no HTML pages, such as an HTTP API, may instead answer a 4xx other than 429: RFC 9309 reads an unavailable robots.txt as allow-all, while Google's crawlers read a 429 as a server error and stop crawling. It never answers 200 with an HTML body, such as a single-page app's fallback route: an HTML body carries no groups and no Sitemap line, so the file is served and says nothing.

No WAF, CDN or edge rule blocks or challenges public routes by User-Agent token or bot category for search-index or user-initiated agents; rate limits apply to them as to any other client. User-initiated fetchers can ignore robots.txt, so for them the edge is the effective access control. A rule that must single out automated traffic exempts these agents by the operator's published IP ranges or a verified-bot signal, never by the User-Agent string alone.

Reachability is checked live as content.probe defines: GET / and /robots.txt once per search-index and user-initiated token in agent_fetchers with the token in the User-Agent header, and once with a User-Agent that names no roster token. Each tokened request answers the status the untokened request gets on the same path, and never a 401, 403 or 429 or a challenge that the untokened request does not get; where /robots.txt answers 200, it permits / for the token. The probe exercises edge rules keyed on the User-Agent header. Where the edge blocks a tokened request through a rule keyed on the operator's published IP ranges or a verified-bot signal, the probe's client sits outside those ranges, so confirm the rule by reading the edge configuration under edge-admits-agents and record the probe result as explained, not as a violation.
